thesis: This episode argues that Visa is a dominant global payment network built on an open-loop strategy that offers superior scalability compared to closed-loop competitors like Amex. The core investment case rests on Visa's incredible profitability, characterized by 98% gross margins and 50% net income margins, driven by a high-throughput infrastructure that processes hundreds of millions of daily transactions with minimal variable costs. Despite competition from tech giants, the thesis suggests Visa remains a strong bull case because true disintermediation would require competitors to become banks, and the company continues to expand its value-added services and digital footprint.

claims.claim: Visa became the dominant global payment card network due to a growth hack involving name changes and regulatory mandates that forced banks to migrate.
claims.quote: really pulling away and becoming, at least for many decades, the dominant global payment card network. The name change ends up becoming this incredible growth hack, because what happens is they're the new operating regulations now that mandate that all cards out there, all the previous BankAmericards need to be migrated to Visa cards

claims.claim: Visa's open-loop network of networks strategy provided far more scalability than closed-loop systems like Amex.
claims.quote: Visa adopts this strategy of the network of networks. They go sign up one bank, that bank can go sign up 100 million customers or 2 million merchants. They get so much scale leverage on signing up just one bank that this strategy makes it so that they have far more scalability than something like AmEx.

claims.claim: Amex is highly regulated because it is a bank on both sides of the transaction, acting as both a card issuing bank and a merchant acquiring bank.
claims.quote: Amex also is a bank themselves, so it's highly regulated. They're a bank by this point in history, I believe, on both sides of the transaction. They're both a card issuing bank, and they are a merchant acquiring bank.

claims.claim: Visa and MasterCard are the dominant way versus closed-loop systems because of their scalability and open-loop nature.
claims.quote: it does potentially come with much better scalability, which is the reason why Visa and MasterCard have become the dominant way versus the closed-loop systems.

claims.claim: Visa realized the opportunity to build an instant global payment network that a large percentage of global commerce runs on.
claims.quote: To actually realize what he sold to Bank of America and the other banks of an instant global payment network that a large percentage of global commerce runs on, you had to build a lot of technology to make that happen.

claims.claim: Visa has achieved incredible dominance in revenue, transactions, and volume over the last decade, with 50% net income margins and 98% gross margins.
claims.quote: the last decade has been the story of Visa's incredible dominance in revenue, in transactions, and in volume. It's just actually true that a lot of their growth has been recent in the last decade.

claims.claim: Visa has 50% net income margins, making it the most profitable large-scale company in the world.
claims.quote: The most shocking thing about the business is they have 50% net income margins. Of the $30-ish billion that they made in revenue, their net income was $15 billion.

claims.claim: Visa has 98% gross margins with no variable costs or cost of goods sold.
claims.quote: Their gross margins are 98%. There are no variable costs in this business. There are no cost of goods sold. It's crazy.

claims.claim: Visa has built high throughput infrastructure globally with 99.999% uptime and almost no downtime.
claims.quote: A big takeaway should be like, my God, they have built high throughput infrastructure globally. That's an unbelievably impressive thing. With almost no downtime, it is 99.999% uptime, which I am not a site reliability engineer, but I think that is five nines.

claims.claim: Visa processes 707 million transactions per day, or 8600 transactions per second.
claims.quote: Visa does 707 million transactions per day. That is 8600 transactions per second, every second throughout the year.

claims.claim: Visa operates six data centers distributed across the world, which is impressive given the reliability and uptime.
claims.quote: They have six data centers distributed across the world. It's amazing it's only six, to be honest, with that kind of reliability and uptime.

claims.claim: Visa connects 16,000 banks in 200 countries.
claims.quote: That's 16,000 banks in 200 countries. They have six data centers distributed across the world.

claims.claim: Visa has 27,000 employees.
claims.quote: They do have 27,000 employees. In some ways, it feels an oddly large number. In other ways, it feels small, but I think we should talk about that in the context of the value added services.

claims.claim: Visa's net revenue is $29 billion, up from $22 billion two years ago.
claims.quote: Their net revenue is $29 billion. That's up from $22 billion two years ago.

claims.claim: Visa has 4.1 billion cards in circulation.
claims.quote: There are 4.1 billion Visa cards in circulation.

claims.claim: Visa's value added services were $6 billion.
claims.quote: Their value added services—this is an interesting thing that I want to come back to—was $6 billion.

claims.claim: US merchants paid an estimated $93 billion in Visa and MasterCard credit card fees last year.
claims.quote: US merchants paid an estimated $93 billion in Visa and MasterCard credit card fees last year according to the Nielsen report and industry publication.

claims.claim: Visa's interchange fees have been reduced from 7% to around 2.24% for in-person transactions.
claims.quote: There has been downward pressure on interchange for a long time. I think industry average right now is down around 2.24, which is compelling considering we started at 7%.

claims.claim: Tokenization allows Visa to create proprietary services with high margins and represents a huge milestone for the transition to digital.
claims.quote: Visa's quote on this is, "This marks a huge milestone, both for the transition to digital and in our work to secure the wider payments ecosystem. And you better bet that that's good for long-term margins and layering products later on."

claims.claim: Visa has a massive Total Addressable Market (TAM) in payments of $200 trillion, with significant opportunities in B2B and B2C sectors.
claims.quote: Here's Visa's version. All of payments is about $200 trillion of volume, and cards are only $20 trillion. Here, we've been playing in this tiny little fraction of the available market. There are a few things that they call out that they want to move into, that B2B payments is about $120 trillion if they can access it.

claims.claim: Visa's bull case is so strong that the hosts suggest reading the annual report to see the full extent of it.
claims.quote: David, these bull cases are so easy. You should read the annual report. The whole thing's a bull case.

claims.claim: Visa remains a bull case today despite competition from Apple and Google, as those companies would likely need to become banks to truly disintermediate Visa.
claims.quote: Ben: It's a bull case today. David: Yeah, it's a bull case today. There may be nuance that I'm missing here, but if you play out how Apple decides, okay, we want to go after Visa, I'm not sure how Apple could actually do that really without becoming a bank themselves.
